key_terms.meaning: An equation in an unknown function of two or more variables and its partial derivatives, e.g. z_x + z_y = z.
A letter like a or b in a relation that can take any fixed value; differentiating removes one constant per differentiation.
An unspecified function like f(u) or φ(x−y); removing it needs differentiation with respect to both x and y and then elimination.
Order = order of the highest derivative present; degree = power of the highest derivative after the equation is made polynomial in derivatives.
p and q appear with no x, y, z; put q = a, solve for p = φ(a), then integrate dz = φ(a)dx + a dy.

key_terms.term: Standard type II: f(z, p, q) = 0
key_terms.meaning: x and y absent; take u = x + ay, so p = dz/du and q = a dz/du, giving an ODE in z and u.

key_terms.term: Standard type III: f(x, p) = g(y, q)
key_terms.meaning: Variables separate; each side equals a constant a, giving two ODEs for p and q.
z = px + qy + f(p, q); the complete integral is z = ax + by + f(a, b).
A solution containing as many arbitrary constants as the number of independent variables (two here), with no special relation forced between them.
A linear first-order PDE Pp + Qq = R, where P, Q, R are functions of x, y, z and p = z_x, q = z_y.
The simultaneous ODEs dx/P = dy/Q = dz/R whose two independent integrals u = c₁, v = c₂ build the solution.
Functions l, m, n chosen so that lP + mQ + nR = 0, making l dx + m dy + n dz = 0 exact and giving a first integral.
The surface z = φ(x, y) that satisfies the PDE at every point; the general solution is F(u, v) = 0.
dx/f_p = dy/f_q = dz/(pf_p + qf_q) = −dp/(f_x + pf_z) = −dq/(f_y + qf_z) for f(x, y, z, p, q) = 0.
Use Charpit's equations to get a second relation between p and q, then integrate the exact differential dz = p dx + q dy.
Find the integral surface of a first-order PDE that passes through a given initial curve with given values of z along it, e.g. z = f(s) on x = x₀(s), y = y₀(s).
A curve in space along which the PDE becomes a chain of ODEs; for Pp + Qq = R it satisfies dx/P = dy/Q = dz/R.
P dx + Q dy + R dz = 0, where P, Q, R are functions of x, y, z; its solution is a one-parameter family of surfaces.
P(R_y − Q_z) + Q(P_z − R_x) + R(Q_x − P_y) = 0; necessary and sufficient for P dx + Q dy + R dz = 0 to have a solution.
P dx + Q dy + R dz = du for some u; then P = u_x, Q = u_y, R = u_z and the solution is u = c.

takeaways: A relation with n arbitrary constants or functions needs n differentiations before the arbitrary elements can be removed, and that is how a PDE is formed.
Each of the four standard types is solved by one fixed substitution that turns the PDE into an ODE.
Lagrange's method reduces a linear PDE to two ordinary first integrals of dx/P = dy/Q = dz/R, and the answer is F(u, v) = 0.
Charpit's method is the general tool: it works where the standard types fail, by building a second relation between p and q.
Every solution of a first-order PDE is a surface, and each arbitrary constant in the complete integral gives a different member of the family.
The Cauchy problem selects one surface out of the family by demanding that it contains a given initial curve.
A Pfaffian equation P dx + Q dy + R dz = 0 is solvable only when the integrability (curl) condition holds; then it represents surfaces orthogonal to the curves dx/P = dy/Q = dz/R.
Numerically, the method of lines converts the PDE into a system of ODEs in one variable and RK4 marches the initial curve forward.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit almost always ask for a full solution step by step: state the type or method, show the working of the auxiliary or standard-type reduction, and write the final answer as a family F(u, v) = 0 or z = ax + by + c.

bank.q: Define order and degree of a partial differential equation. Form the PDE by eliminating the arbitrary constants a and b from (x − a)² + (y − b)² + z² = c², where c is a fixed constant, and state its order, degree and type.
outline: Order = 2, degree = 1; explain both from the final equation.
Differentiate once w.r.t. x: (x − a) + z z_x = 0; differentiate once w.r.t. y: (y − b) + z z_y = 0.
Eliminate a and b using the original relation to get z²(p² + q² + 1) = c².
Check: no arbitrary constant remains, so the PDE is of the second order and first degree.

bank.q: Explain the four standard types of first-order nonlinear PDEs. For each type, give the form, the substitution used, and the ODE it leads to.
outline: Type I f(p, q) = 0: take q = a, solve for p, integrate dz = φ(a) dx + a dy.
Type II f(z, p, q) = 0: take u = x + ay, p = dz/du, q = a dz/du, get an ODE in z and u.
Type III f(x, p) = g(y, q): each side equals a constant a, giving two ODEs.
Type IV z = px + qy + f(p, q) (Clairaut): complete integral z = ax + by + f(a, b).
Mention that each substitution removes one independent variable.

bank.q: State Charpit's auxiliary equations for f(x, y, z, p, q) = 0 and explain the role of each equation. Show how the method ends with the integration of dz = p dx + q dy.
outline: Write the five-term chain dx/f_p = dy/f_q = dz/(pf_p + qf_q) = −dp/(f_x + p f_z) = −dq/(f_y + q f_z).
Explain that the chain comes from requiring dz − p dx − q dy = 0 together with df = 0.
Choose the pair of fractions easiest to integrate to get a relation between p and q.
Substitute back to make dz = p dx + q dy exact, then integrate to get the complete integral with two constants.

bank.q: State the necessary and sufficient condition of integrability for the Pfaffian equation P dx + Q dy + R dz = 0, and explain what the condition means in vector language.
outline: Write P(R_y − Q_z) + Q(P_z − R_x) + R(Q_x − P_y) = 0.
Show that for an exact form this reduces to equality of mixed second derivatives.
Vector form: if F = (P, Q, R) then F · curl F = 0.
Use it to test a given equation before attempting a solution.

bank.q: Form the PDE by eliminating the arbitrary function f from z = f(x² + y²) and hence solve the resulting first-order equation.
outline: Differentiate w.r.t. x: p = 2x f′(x² + y²); w.r.t. y: q = 2y f′.
Eliminate f′ to get y p − x q = 0.
Solve as a Lagrange equation with auxiliary system dx/y = dy/(−x) = dz/0.
First integral x² + y² = c₁ from x dx + y dy = 0; second integral z = c₂.
General solution z = F(x² + y²).
This is standard type I, f(p, q) = 0.
Put q = a², so p = (1 − a)².
Then dz = (1 − a)² dx + a² dy.
Integrate: z = (1 − a)² x + a² y + c.
State clearly that a and c are the two arbitrary constants.
Recognise Clairaut's form z = px + qy + f(p, q) with f = p²q².
Complete integral: z = ax + by + a²b².
Verify by direct substitution.
Note that the singular solution, if asked, comes from eliminating a and b from the complete integral and its a- and b-derivatives.

bank.q: Solve (mz − ny)p + (nx − lz)q = ly − mx, where l, m, n are constants.
outline: Identify P = mz − ny, Q = nx − lz, R = ly − mx.
Use multipliers l, m, n: lP + mQ + nR = 0, so l dx + m dy + n dz = 0.
First integral: lx + my + nz = c₁.
Use multipliers x, y, z: x dx + y dy + z dz = 0.
Second integral: x² + y² + z² = c₂.
General solution: F(lx + my + nz, x² + y² + z²) = 0.

bank.q: Using Charpit's method, solve p²x + q²y = z.
outline: Take f = p²x + q²y − z = 0, compute f_x = p², f_y = q², f_z = −1, f_p = 2px, f_q = 2qy.
Write Charpit's chain and simplify to dp/p = dq/q (or the equivalent usable pair).
Get p = aq, then substitute back: q²(ax + y) = z, so q = √(z/(ax + y)).
Form dz = p dx + q dy and integrate.
Report the complete integral with constants a and c.

bank.q: Solve the Pfaffian equation yz dx + zx dy + xy dz = 0 and interpret the answer geometrically.
outline: Test integrability, or note directly that the left side is d(xyz).
So xyz = c is the solution.
Each value of c gives one surface; together they form a family of surfaces.
Verify by partial differentiation: P = u_x, Q = u_y, R = u_z with u = xyz.

bank.q: Solve p + q = 1 subject to z = x on the line y = 0 (a Cauchy problem).
outline: Characteristics satisfy dx/1 = dy/1 = dz/1.
Two first integrals: x − y = c₁, z − x = c₂.
General solution z = x + G(x − y).
Impose z = x at y = 0: G(x) = 0, so z = x.
Check that the initial curve is nowhere tangent to the characteristics, otherwise the data are not admissible.

bank.q: For the Pfaffian equation P dx + Q dy + R dz = 0, prove that its integral surfaces are orthogonal to the curves of the simultaneous system dx/P = dy/Q = dz/R, and use this to compare the two problems.
outline: Let the integral surface be u(x, y, z) = c, so du = u_x dx + u_y dy + u_z dz = 0 with (u_x, u_y, u_z) parallel to (P, Q, R).
A tangent direction (dx, dy, dz) of the curve system is also parallel to (P, Q, R).
The normal to the surface and the curve direction are therefore the same line, so the curves cut the surfaces at right angles.
Conclude that solving the Pfaffian equation and solving the simultaneous equations are dual problems, related by the integrability condition.

bank.q: Show that when the PDE is linear in p and q, Charpit's method reduces to Lagrange's method, and explain why Charpit is the more general tool.
outline: Take f = Pp + Qq − R with P, Q, R free of p and q.
Then f_p = P, f_q = Q, and f_x + p f_z, f_y + q f_z give the Lagrange-type fractions.
Show that the p and q equations become the same as the dx/P = dy/Q = dz/R chain.
Conclude that Lagrange handles only the linear case; Charpit also covers nonlinear equations with no standard-type substitution.

bank.q: For the first-order PDE z_x = z_y with the initial data z = f(x) on y = 0, discuss existence, uniqueness and how the method of lines with fourth-order Runge–Kutta would compute the solution numerically.
outline: Characteristics: dx/1 = dy/(−1) = dz/0, so x + y = c and z is constant along them.
Solution z = f(x + y) exists and is unique when f is differentiable.
Method of lines: replace z_y by a finite difference on a y-grid, giving a system of ODEs in x (or vice versa) for the grid values.
March with RK4 using step h; the local error per step is O(h⁵) and the global error is O(h⁴).
Note that a discontinuity in f is carried along the characteristic x + y = constant, which can spoil the numerical solution.

glossary.def: An equation relating an unknown function of several variables to its partial derivatives.
The order of the highest partial derivative appearing in the equation.
The exponent of the highest-order derivative after the equation is cleared of radicals and fractions in derivatives.
A PDE in which the unknown and all its derivatives appear only to the first power and never multiplied together.
A symbol standing for a fixed but unspecified number, removed from a relation by differentiation.
An unspecified function of a combination of variables, removed by differentiating with respect to each variable and eliminating.
A solution containing two independent arbitrary constants for a PDE in two independent variables.
A solution obtained from the complete integral by giving fixed numerical values to its arbitrary constants.
A solution not obtainable from the complete integral by fixing constants; it is the envelope of the family of surfaces.
The solution written as F(u, v) = 0, where F is an arbitrary function and u, v are first integrals.
The PDE z = px + qy + f(p, q), whose complete integral is z = ax + by + f(a, b).
A first-order PDE linear in p and q, written Pp + Qq = R.
The simultaneous system dx/P = dy/Q = dz/R used to solve a Lagrange equation.
A factor used with the auxiliary equations so that the sum of the numerators becomes an exact differential.
The surface z = φ(x, y) formed by the graph of a solution of the PDE.
A curve along which the PDE reduces to ordinary differential equations.
A general method that builds a second relation between p and q and then integrates dz = p dx + q dy.
A given space curve through which the required integral surface must pass.
The problem of finding the integral surface of a PDE that contains a prescribed initial curve.
An equation P dx + Q dy + R dz = 0 relating three variables through a total differential.
The identity P(R_y − Q_z) + Q(P_z − R_x) + R(Q_x − P_y) = 0 that a Pfaffian form must satisfy.
A form P dx + Q dy + R dz that equals du for some function u.
Solving a first-order PDE by following the characteristic curves from the initial data.
Replacing the derivatives in one variable by finite differences so the PDE becomes a system of ODEs in the other variable.
